title: Whoever Responds First Usually Wins
content:
###  **The Finding** 

Research from Lead Connect found that 78 percent of customers hire the company that responds first. 

Not the cheapest. Not the highest rated. The first one to get back to them. 

###  **Why This Is More True Than It Used to Be** 

Homeowners now expect fast replies as a baseline, and they usually contact more than one company. Housecall Pro found that 72 percent of homeowners would pay more to resolve an emergency within 24 hours — speed is not only a tiebreaker, it carries a premium. 

Meanwhile CallRail has reported a missed call rate in home services in the range of 14 percent. Roughly one in seven calls to home service businesses goes unanswered. 

###  **The Uncomfortable Implication** 

If response speed decides most jobs, then a company with fewer leads and disciplined follow-up will outperform a company with more leads and slower follow-up — reliably, and by a wide margin. 

Which means buying more leads is frequently the wrong response to a slow month. The leads already purchased may not have been worked. 

### **The Part Nobody Wants to Audit** 

The most useful number most contractors do not track: what percentage of leads received were contacted at all, and how quickly. 

That figure often explains more about channel performance than lead quality does. A channel judged as poor is sometimes a channel that was never worked. 

**\## Where We Sit on This** 

We track when a lead was delivered and whether the client contacted it, because otherwise there is no way to tell a lead-quality problem from a follow-up problem. It is a slightly uncomfortable thing to measure in both directions, which is precisely why it is worth measuring.
